tip.title: mon, ma or mes?
tip.body: Use mon with masculine words (mon père, mon frère), ma with feminine words (ma mère, ma sœur) and mes for any plural (mes parents). Voici means "here is / this is" when you show someone. Pronunciation: the final -s of mes and the final -e of mère, père, frère are silent (but the r is pronounced), and these three words rhyme.

tip.title: grand, grande — hear the ending
tip.body: Adjectives agree with the person: il est grand, elle est grande. Often the feminine -e makes a silent consonant come alive: grand [gʁɑ̃] → grande [gʁɑ̃d], petit → petite (you hear the t). Adjectives that already end in -e don't change: drôle, timide. Sympa doesn't change either. il = he, elle = she.

phrases.note: French uses avoir for age: literally "he has ten years".
les yeux is said with a liaison: [le-zyø].
In everyday speech on usually means "we".

tip.title: Papi, mamie — c'est or ce sont?
tip.body: Grand-père and grand-mère are the standard words; at home children say papi (or papy) and mamie. Les grands-parents = grandparents. For one person say C'est …, for several people Ce sont … (in casual speech many people also say C'est mes grands-parents). Pets: un chien (dog), un chat (cat) — the final -n and -t are silent.

lessons.title: mon, ton, son, votre
lessons.goal: Say my, your, his and her with the right form.

tip.title: Possessives agree with the thing owned
tip.body: my: mon / ma / mes · your (tu): ton / ta / tes · his or her: son / sa / ses · your (vous): votre / vos. The form depends on the noun, not on the owner: son père can mean his father or her father; sa mère is his or her mother. Before a feminine word starting with a vowel sound, use mon/ton/son to avoid a clash: mon amie, ton école. In the plural, liaison is heard: mes_amis, ses_enfants, vos_enfants. Use ton/ta/tes with a friend, votre/vos with someone you say vous to.

culture.title: Le repas du dimanche
culture.body: In many French families the Sunday lunch is a tradition: grandparents, parents and children gather around the table, often for a long meal that can stretch well into the afternoon. Within the family people generally use tu, including with parents and grandparents. Watch out for meal names: in France le déjeuner is lunch and le dîner is the evening meal, but in Belgium, Switzerland and Québec people usually say le déjeuner for breakfast, le dîner for lunch and le souper for the evening meal.
